card.title: Electric field and electric field intensity due to point …

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Field intensity is force per unit positive charge. A point charge gives kQ/r^2, a long line gives a field that falls as 1/r, and an infinite insulating sheet gives the constant field σ/(2ε0). Just outside a conductor the field is σ/ε0.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
F = k q₁q₂/r²
E = F/q
∮E·dA = Q/ε₀

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ state the rule without its limit → ✅ note when it applies / stops applying.  ·  ❌ no diagram → ✅ add one labelled figure / structured list.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Electric field intensity is the force on a small positive test charge divided by that charge. Its unit is the newton per coulomb. The test charge must be small enough not to disturb the sources.  ·  A point charge Q produces E = k Q / r^2, outward if Q is positive. Two point charges need a vector sum. On the perpendicular bisector of an equal and opposite pair, the fields point the same way along the bisector.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: electric field, electric field intensity due to point charges, line charges, charged sheets (within Electrostatics).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Physics — don't mix them.

rows.text: Point: 1/r^2. Line: 1/r. Sheet: constant.  ·  Conductor surface: σ/ε0. Insulating sheet: σ/(2ε0).

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Point-charge field  ·  Line charge  ·  Infinite sheet  ·  Conductor surface

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: • Electric field intensity due to point charges  ·  Field is force per unit positive charge.  ·  A point charge falls as 1/r^2.  ·  A long line falls as 1/r.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Coulomb: F = (1/4πε₀)·q₁q₂/r². Electric field E = F/q = kq/r²; for a line/dipole use superposition.  ·  Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀ — powerful for spherical/cylindrical/planar symmetry.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: What is E for an infinite non-conducting sheet?

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: An infinite non-conducting sheet has σ = 1.77 × 10^−8 C/m^2. Take 2 ε0 = 1.77 × 10^−11. Find E and its direction if σ is positive.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A point-charge field falls as → B  ·  A long line of charge has a field that falls as → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: A long straight line of charge uses Gauss's law. The field is radial and E = λ / (2 π ε0 r), so it falls as 1/r rather than 1/r^2. λ is the charge per unit length.  ·  An infinite non-conducting sheet with surface charge density σ produces a field σ / (2 ε0) on each side, pointing away from the sheet if σ is positive. The field does not fall with distance in this ideal infinite case.  ·  A conducting sheet with the same charge density on one outer surface has E = σ / ε0 just outside, because the conductor forces the field lines to leave from one side in the standard result for a thin charged conductor.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: V = kq/r  ·  An infinite sheet gives a constant field.  ·  ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ coulomb: f = (1/4πε₀)·q₁q₂/r². electric field e = f/q = kq/r²; for a line/dipole use superposition..

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The sheet field is not k Q / r^2.  ·  The line field falls as 1/r, not 1/r^2.  ·  σ / (2 ε0) is the non-conducting sheet. A conductor surface is σ / ε0.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: E is not the force. The force is q E.  ·  Name the shape before the formula.  ·  Give the direction: away from positive charge.
